title: Interactive rebase
description: Learn about Interactive rebase. Master the concepts, patterns, and best practices.

data.text: Interactive rebase lets you rewrite commit history before it is shared. You can reorder, edit, squash, fixup, or drop commits, producing a clean narrative that is easier to review and maintain.

data.title: Lesson Scope
data.text: This lesson covers interactive rebase operations, the golden rule of rebasing, splitting commits, and safety considerations when rewriting public history.
Interactive rebase opens an editor listing commits and available actions. You tell Git how each commit should be treated, and Git replays the history accordingly.

data.title: Starting an Interactive Rebase
data.code: git rebase -i HEAD~5

data.text: When you start an interactive rebase, Git opens your default editor with a todo list. Each line shows a commit hash, subject, and action keyword. The default action is pick, which means include the commit as-is.

data.title: Rebase Todo List
data.code:
pick abc1234 feat(auth): add login endpoint
pick def5678 fix(auth): validate email format
pick ghi9012 chore: update dependencies
pick jkl3456 feat(api): add user profile route
pick mno7890 test(auth): add login tests

data.text: Pick includes the commit in the final history without changes. Use pick when the commit is already clean and correctly ordered.

data.title: Keeping a Commit with Pick
data.code: pick abc1234 feat(auth): add login endpoint

data.text: Reword lets you edit the commit message during the rebase. The commit content stays the same, but the message can be improved for clarity or to match conventions.

data.title: Rewording a Commit Message
data.code:
reword def5678 fix(auth): validate email format

# Git opens the editor for you to edit the message

data.text: Squash combines a commit with the one above it, merging their changes and prompting you to write a new combined message. Use squash for commits that are part of the same logical change but were committed separately.

data.title: Squashing Two Commits
data.code:
pick abc1234 feat(auth): add login endpoint
squash def5678 fix(auth): validate email format

# After squash, you write a combined message:

data.title: Squash for Clean History
data.text: Squash trivial fixup commits into the main feature commit before opening a pull request. This keeps the review history focused on meaningful changes.
Fixup is like squash, but it discards the fixup commit's message entirely. The fixup changes are merged into the previous commit, and the message remains unchanged. Use fixup for small corrections.

data.title: Using Fixup
data.code:
pick abc1234 feat(auth): add login endpoint
fixup def5678 fix(auth): typo in validation logic

# def5678 changes are folded into abc1234
# Message remains: feat(auth): add login endpoint

data.text: Drop removes a commit from the history entirely. Use drop when a commit should never have been made, such as a committed secret or a large accidental file addition.

data.title: Dropping a Commit
data.code:
pick abc1234 feat(auth): add login endpoint
drop def5678 chore: accidentally committed .env file

data.title: Dropped Commits Are Still in Reflog
data.text: Even if you drop a commit during rebase, the original commit may still exist in the reflog. Use git gc to prune unreachable objects if the dropped commit contained sensitive data.
Edit pauses the rebase at a specific commit, letting you modify the changes or the message. After fixing the commit, run git rebase --continue to proceed.

data.title: Editing a Commit
data.code:
pick abc1234 feat(auth): add login endpoint
edit def5678 fix(auth): validate email format

# Rebase pauses at def5678
# Make your changes
git add .
git commit --amend

git rebase --continue

data.text: Simply rearrange the lines in the rebase todo list to reorder commits. Git replays them in the new order. Be careful when reordering commits that modify the same file, as conflicts may arise.

data.title: Reordering Commits
data.code:
# Original order
pick abc1234 feat(auth): add login endpoint
pick def5678 chore: update dependencies
pick ghi9012 fix(auth): validate email format

# New order
pick abc1234 feat(auth): add login endpoint
pick ghi9012 fix(auth): validate email format
pick def5678 chore: update dependencies

data.text: To split one commit into multiple logical commits, mark it as edit. When rebase pauses, reset the commit but keep the changes staged. Then stage and commit each logical piece separately.

data.title: Splitting a Commit
data.code:
pick abc1234 feat(auth): add login and password reset
edit def5678 fix(auth): validate both forms

# At the edit step
git reset HEAD^

git add src/auth/login.ts
git commit -m "feat(auth): add login endpoint"

git add src/auth/password-reset.ts
git commit -m "feat(auth): add password reset flow"

git rebase --continue

data.title: Split Before Sharing
data.text: Split commits locally before pushing to a shared branch. Once a commit is public, rewriting it forces all collaborators to re-sync.

If you notice an issue in an older commit but have already made new commits on top, you can use git rebase -i with the fixup action. The fixup commit merges into the target commit, cleaning up history without changing the target message.

data.title: Fixing an Older Commit
data.code:
# Latest commit fixes a typo in an earlier commit
git commit -m "fix(auth): typo in error message"

# Start interactive rebase including the fixup commit
git rebase -i HEAD~3

# In the editor:
pick abc1234 feat(auth): add login
fixup def5678 fix(auth): typo in error message

data.text: Never rebase commits that have already been pushed to a shared or public branch. Rewriting shared history creates divergent histories, forces collaborators to re-merge or re-base, and can cause data loss.

data.title: Golden Rule
data.text: Rebase only local, unpushed commits. Once a commit exists on origin or another developer's clone, treat it as immutable.
Before opening a pull request, rebase your feature branch onto the latest main. This produces a linear history and lets you resolve conflicts in small, reviewable steps.

data.title: Rebasing onto Main
data.code:
git checkout feature/auth-improvements
git fetch origin
git rebase origin/main

# If conflicts occur, fix and continue
git add .
git rebase --continue

data.text: Conflicts during rebase happen when the same lines were changed in both the branch and the base. Git pauses and marks the conflicted files. Resolve them, stage the fixes, and continue the rebase.

data.title: Resolving Rebase Conflicts
data.code:
# After conflict
git status

# Edit conflicted files, then
git add resolved-file.ts

git rebase --continue

data.title: Do Not Force Push During an Active Rebase
data.text: Wait until the rebase finishes before pushing. If you need to update the remote branch, force push only after the local rebase is complete.
If a rebase goes wrong, abort it to return to the original branch state. This is safer than trying to manually untangle a broken rebase.

data.title: Aborting a Rebase
data.code: git rebase --abort

data.text: To squash an entire branch into a single commit, use git rebase -i with the squash or fixup action on every commit except the first. The first commit becomes the single squashed commit.

data.title: Squashing Entire Branch
data.code:
git rebase -i main

# In the editor, change all but the first line from pick to squash

data.text: On GitHub and GitLab, you can update a pull request branch by force pushing after a rebase. The pull request updates automatically, preserving reviews and comments.

data.title: Force Push After Rebase
data.code: git push origin feature/auth-improvements --force-with-lease

data.title: Use --force-with-lease
data.text: --force-with-lease refuses to overwrite the remote branch if someone else pushed in the meantime, preventing accidental data loss.

cards.title: History Shape
cards.description: Rebase: linear. Merge: graph with merge commits.

cards.title: Safety
cards.description: Rebase: risky on shared branches. Merge: safe everywhere.

cards.title: Conflict Frequency
cards.description: Rebase: conflicts may repeat per commit. Merge: conflicts once.

cards.title: Traceability
cards.description: Rebase: clean but obscures original branch boundaries. Merge: preserves branch context.

items: Rebasing a branch that has already been pushed and pulled by teammates
Forgetting to resolve conflicts before continuing the rebase
Accidentally dropping commits by editing the wrong lines in the todo list
Rebasing without testing afterward, assuming the result is correct

data.title: Always Test After Rebase
data.text: A rebase rewrites commits. Even if the original branch passed tests, the rebased result may introduce subtle issues. Run the test suite after every rebase.
Interactive rebase is essential for producing professional commit histories. Use it locally to organize work before sharing, but never rewrite commits that already exist on a shared remote.

data.title: Key Takeaways
text: Use pick, reword, squash, fixup, edit, and drop to shape history
Never rebase commits that are already on a shared branch
Force push with --force-with-lease after local rebase
Run the full test suite after every rebase

data.text: Interactive rebase opens an editor where you can pick, reword, squash, fixup, edit, or drop commits. It is the Swiss Army knife of local history editing.
Rebase moves commits to a new base. Reset moves the branch pointer and optionally the working tree. Use rebase when you want to keep changes; use reset when you want to discard them.

data.title: Reset vs Rebase
data.code:
# Reset discards commits
git reset --hard HEAD~2

# Rebase replays commits onto a new base
git rebase -i HEAD~5

data.text: You can rebase onto any commit, not just HEAD~N. Use git merge-base to find the common ancestor and rebase from there. This is useful when integrating a long-running feature branch.

data.title: Rebase onto Merge Base
data.code:
BASE=$(git merge-base feature/auth main)

git rebase -i $BASE

data.text: By default, rebase flattens merge commits. Use git rebase -r or --rebase-merges to preserve the branch topology while still rewriting commit messages or squashing fixups.

data.title: Rebase with Merge Preservation
data.code: git rebase -r -i origin/main

data.text: The -x flag runs a command after each commit during rebase. This is useful for running tests after every commit to catch breakage early.

data.title: Running Tests After Each Commit
data.code: git rebase -i -x "npm test" origin/main

data.text: Git's autosquash feature automatically moves fixup and squash commits to the correct position during rebase. Generate fixup commits with git commit --fixup <SHA> and let Git handle the rest.

data.title: Using Autosquash
data.code:
# Create a fixup commit
git commit --fixup abc1234

# Rebase with autosquash
git rebase -i --autosquash origin/main

data.text: You can choose a merge strategy during rebase with -s. The recursive strategy is the default, but you can use ort or resolve for specific scenarios.

data.title: Choosing a Rebase Strategy
data.code: git rebase -s ort -i origin/main

data.text: If your team uses signed commits, use git rebase -S to re-sign each commit during rebase. Without -S, the rebased commits lose their signatures.

data.title: Rebase with Signed Commits
data.code: git rebase -S -i origin/main

data.text: Git worktrees are unaffected by rebases in other worktrees. You can run a long rebase in one worktree while continuing normal work in another.

data.title: Using Worktrees During Rebase
data.code:
git worktree add /tmp/rebase-worktree feature/auth

# Rebase in the worktree while main worktree stays on main

data.text: If you have uncommitted changes during a rebase, Git may stash them automatically or abort the rebase. Use git stash push -u to include untracked files, and git stash pop after the rebase.

data.title: Stashing During Rebase
data.code:
git stash push -u -m "wip before rebase"

git rebase -i origin/main

git stash pop

data.text: Rebasing commits that modify binary files can be tricky. Git handles binary files by choosing the latest version, but you may need to resolve conflicts manually if both sides changed the binary.

data.title: Binary Files and Rebase
data.text: Git cannot auto-merge binary files. If a rebase hits a binary conflict, decide which version to keep and stage it.
Rebasing a large number of commits can be slow. Use git rebase --onto to skip unnecessary commits, or use git merge instead if the branch is far behind.

data.title: Skipping Commits During Rebase
data.code:
git rebase --onto origin/main abc1234 feature/auth

# Rebases only commits after abc1234 onto origin/main

data.text: Some teams run CI on every push, including force pushes after rebase. This ensures the rebased branch still passes all checks before reviewers evaluate it.

data.title: CI Triggered by Force Push
data.code:
on:
  push:
    branches: [feature/*]
  pull_request:

data.text: GitHub draft pull requests are great for work-in-progress. You can rebase a draft PR as many times as needed. Once the PR is marked ready for review, the history should be clean.

items: Use draft PRs for early feedback
Rebase frequently to stay up to date with main
Clean up history before marking the PR ready
Request review only after the history is tidy

data.text: On teams that allow rebasing, communicate before force pushing. A force push changes the branch history and can disrupt teammates who have the branch checked out.

items: Post a message in Slack before force pushing
Use --force-with-lease to avoid overwriting others' work
Wait for CI to pass before considering the rebase complete
Do not rebase branches that have open pull requests from other contributors

data.text: GitLab and Bitbucket also support rebase and merge. The mechanics are the same as GitHub. Check your platform's documentation for platform-specific options.

items: GitLab: Settings > General > Merge method > Rebase merge
Bitbucket: Repository settings > Workflow > Merge strategy > Rebase
All platforms: use --force-with-lease when pushing after rebase
